name: AGI Hype Comparison
subject: quantum-computing
subjectTitle: A Skeptic's Guide to Quantum Computing

lesson.title: The Next Five Years, Forever: AGI Hype and the Quantum Echo
lesson.summary: Predictions that human level artificial general intelligence is a handful of years away have been made confidently and repeatedly across multiple distinct eras of AI research, and the recurring gap between those predictions and reality offers another clean case study in the same hype pattern this course has been teaching you to recognize.
lesson.body:
Artificial intelligence research has, across several distinct eras, produced genuine breakthroughs, followed by public predictions that human level general intelligence was close at hand, followed by periods where progress toward that specific goal slowed and enthusiasm cooled, sometimes described within the field itself as an AI winter, followed later by a new wave of genuine capability jumps and a fresh round of confident near term predictions. The specific details differ across eras, but the shape of the pattern repeats closely enough to be instructive.

The parallel to quantum computing is direct once you see it. Both fields combine real, verifiable progress, AI systems keep getting more capable at more tasks, and quantum processors keep scaling up qubit counts and coherence times, with a separate and much shakier claim: that this specific kind of progress, extrapolated forward, gets you all the way to the headline destination on the announced schedule. For AGI that destination is general intelligence matching or exceeding human ability across essentially all cognitive tasks. For quantum computing it is a large scale, fault tolerant, generally useful machine. Progress on measurable capability and progress toward the specific hard destination are not the same measurement, and hype narratives in both fields routinely blur the two together as if closing the gap on one automatically closes the gap on the other.

A specific mechanism shows up in both fields worth naming directly: expert disagreement gets flattened in public discussion. In both AGI and quantum computing, credible, well informed researchers hold genuinely different views about how close the field actually is, some believe the remaining gap is mostly more of the same kind of scaling that has worked so far, others believe it requires conceptual breakthroughs no one has found yet. Popular coverage tends to quote the most bullish available voice as though it represents a consensus that does not actually exist, which is itself one of the red flags in tech claims worth watching for on its own.

The same due diligence and base rate discipline from earlier chapters applies here without modification. Ask what specifically changed versus what was merely extrapolated from a trend line. Ask who is making the prediction and what they personally gain from a punchy timeline, whether that is raising money, attracting talent, drawing policy attention, or building personal prominence. And remember that capability has jumped recently is genuine evidence, but it is evidence that needs to be weighed against the base rate of prior capability jumps that were also followed by confident predictions that did not hold up on schedule, not treated as proof that this time the pattern is finally different.
